title: Ofada Stew
author: Chioma Adeleke
desc: Forty unripe habaneros to two green peppers — the heat-to-sweet ratio inverted — with the puree boiled bone dry before it ever meets the oil.
longDesc: This is the hot one. Where the other ayamase recipes build on five or six green bell peppers with three scotch bonnets for heat, this one uses forty unripe habaneros against just two tatashe, which flips the dish from a sweet green stew with a bite into something the site compares to vindaloo. The technique is different too: the blended peppers are cooked in a separate pot on high heat until all the water dries up, and only then do they go into the bleached oil to fry dry a second time. Twelve minutes on low to medium is the bleaching time, with the oil going clear like vegetable oil.
ingredients: 2 green tatashe peppers or green bell peppers
20 cl red palm oil, at least
850 g assorted meat and fish — beef, shaki, dry fish, stockfish
equipment: Two pots, one clean and dry for the oil
steps: Wash and blend the peppers with the onion, deseeding the tatashe or bell pepper.
Grind the crayfish and the locust bean seasoning in a dry mill.
Cook the meat and fish with a stock cube until done.
Pour the pepper blend into a separate pot and cook on high heat till all the water dries up.
In a clean dry pot, in a well-ventilated kitchen, bleach the palm oil until it turns clear. It should look like vegetable oil when done — about 12 minutes on low to medium heat.
Cool the oil slightly, then add the boiled puree and fry till all the water has dried from the pepper.
Add the crayfish, the locust bean seasoning, and the meat and fish. Stir.
Salt to taste, simmer, and serve.
chefTips: Forty habaneros is not a typo and it is not for everyone. If you want the sweeter green stew, use NGA016 or NGA018 instead.
Ventilate, and do not leave the pot. The source is explicit: the oil will catch fire if overheated. Its other advice — turn off your smoke alarm — is worth ignoring.
The puree is dried twice: once alone on high heat, then again in the oil. That double drying is what concentrates it.
Clear, like vegetable oil, is this source's endpoint. Note that another named source describes the endpoint as the oil 'darkening slightly', which is not the same state at all.
Cool the oil slightly before the puree goes in. Hot oil and wet puree spits violently.
Deseed the tatashe but not the habaneros. The sweet pepper's seeds are bitter; the habanero's are the point.
'1 locust bean seasoning' is printed with no unit. Two heaped tablespoons of iru is the figure other named sources use for a comparable batch.
commonMistakes: Scaling the habaneros down without adjusting anything else, which leaves it thin.
Adding the puree to oil that is still at bleaching temperature.
Skipping the separate dry-off and putting wet puree into the oil.
Bleaching in a pot with any water in it.
sources: Adapted from 'How to cook Ofada Stew (Ayamase)', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 40 pcs unripe habanero peppers, 2 green tatashe peppers or green bell peppers, 1 locust bean seasoning, 20cl red palm oil (at least), 1 big onion, 1 handful crayfish, 850g assorted meat and fish.
The page also glosses the dish 'Ofada Stew (Designers Stew)' and describes it as 'the hottest of them all when it comes to Nigerian hot and spicy food', tasting 'like Vindaloo (Indian Curry)'.
The bleaching figure is as printed: 'It took me 12 minutes on low to medium heat', with 'Your own time may vary', and the endpoint 'it turns clear. It should look like vegetable oil when done'.

SAFETY, verbatim from the page: 'Do so in a well ventilated area. Turn on your kitchen extractor'; 'Do not leave the pot unattended because the oil will catch fire if overheated'; and cool the oil before adding ingredients 'to prevent hot splashes of oil'. The page also advises turning off the smoke alarm, which is not reproduced as advice here.
NOTE: '1 locust bean seasoning' is printed with no unit and is effectively unquantified. LIST/METHOD MISMATCH: stock cube and salt appear only in the method, not in the ingredient list.

DISAGREEMENT on the pepper base, not reconciled: 40 unripe habaneros to 2 tatashe here, against 6 green bell to 3-4 rodo (Sisi Jemimah, NGA016), 5 green bell to 3 scotch bonnet (9jafoodie) and 4 green bell to 2 green chilies plus 2 habanero (Lola Osinkolu, NGA018). The heat-to-sweet ratio in this version is inverted relative to all three others.

DISAGREEMENT on pepper handling: blended raw then boiled dry on high heat (here), oven-roasted whole then blended coarse (NGA016), blended raw then drained in a sieve with no cooking-dry step (9jafoodie).
healthBenefits: Capsaicin from the habaneros is associated with raised thermogenesis.
High protein from the assorted meat and fish.
culturalNote: Ofada stew takes its name from the rice, not the other way round — the sauce itself is ayamase, and ofada is a community in Obafemi Owode Local Government Area in Ogun State whose name became the blanket trade term for almost all locally produced Nigerian rice. One named source argues it should have protected designation of origin status so that real Ofada rice can be told apart from the rest.
